headline: This morning's showers are the last real rain before Monday: HRRR's 15-minute run shows a short burst about 7 to 8 AM (0.26 in, under the 0.40 in alarm) near the 7.9 ft high tide running about 1.5 ft high, and the Saturday cell is gone; no street flooding expected.

summary.text: HRRR's Saturday 4 to 7 PM cell (0.38 in) is gone; its 15-minute run is dry from mid-morning through Saturday night. RRFS dropped Friday morning from 0.22 to 0.05 in.
Wettest 3 hours, next 72 h: HRRR 15-min 0.31 (this morning), NBM 0.14, ECMWF 0.09 (Sat night), RRFS 0.05, GFS 0.04. HRRR hourly data missing. Consensus about 0.14 in (NBM, middle value).
Most likely nothing beyond full gutters. A heavy shower cell could briefly put water on the sidewalk. Yellow (garage) needs about 0.71 in in 3 hours or a 0.40 in hour.
Heaviest showers about 7 to 8 AM, tapering by mid-morning; isolated showers possible this afternoon. Light rain Saturday evening and night, then dry Monday before Tuesday's bigger storm.
This morning's 7.9 ft high at 8:32 AM runs about 9.5 ft on NOAA's Bay model (~1.5 ft surge), overlapping the burst. Channel low: Caltrain 0.18 ft, Alameda 0.27 ft.
No need to move cars. Glance at the page until about 10 AM; use Monday's dry day to clear drain grates and check sandbags before Tuesday's storm and king tides.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: Cold, unstable air on the back side of the departing low keeps scattered to numerous showers going over the Bay Area this morning (NWS San Francisco aviation discussion, 4:28 AM), with a 10% chance of thunderstorms and the best chance of showers through the morning and early afternoon. Showers decrease tonight, though a few could linger into Saturday morning. A weaker system brings light showers to the Bay Area by late Saturday afternoon into Sunday (NWS: a tenth to a quarter inch from Saturday to early Monday), and NWS warns that nearly saturated soils make nuisance flooding more likely if stronger showers develop. Monday is the dry day. A stronger, negatively tilted trough arrives Tuesday into Wednesday with possible thunderstorms and moderate to heavy rain (NWS: 1 to 1.5 in for most of the Bay Area), together with the king tides of November 24 to 26. That storm is still beyond this discussion's 72-hour window.

sections.title: What changed and model trends
sections.text:
Since the 1:30 AM discussion the rain picture for the next three days has shrunk. The HRRR's lone Saturday 4 to 7 PM cell (0.38 in, almost all in one hour) is gone: the newest HRRR 15-minute output is dry from about 9:30 AM Friday through the end of its run late Saturday night. The hourly HRRR series came back empty in this snapshot ("no data"), so its hourly numbers can't be checked this time.

Instead the HRRR 15-minute output brings back a short Friday-morning burst: 0.08 in in the 15 minutes ending 7:00 AM, then 0.06, 0.07 and 0.06 in, about 0.26 in in the hour ending 7:45 AM and 0.31 in in its wettest 3 hours (about 6:45 to 9:45 AM). That is a busy hour but still well under the 0.40 in burst alarm, and it is happening as this is written.

The other models are lighter. RRFS (10 PM Thu run) fell from 0.22 to 0.05 in in its wettest 3 hours (7 to 10 AM), with a top hour of 0.04 in. NBM has 0.14 in for 7 to 10 AM (0.09 in in the hour ending 9 AM), and then only 0.03 to 0.04 in per hour Saturday 4 to 6 PM. ECMWF's wettest stretch is Saturday 7 to 10 PM, 0.09 in (0.03 in per hour). GFS has 0.04 in.

Consensus: with the HRRR 15-minute value (0.31 × 1.25 = 0.39), RRFS 0.05 and NBM 0.14, the middle value is 0.14 in, down from 0.22 in. If the dashboard can't use the HRRR this hour, the figure comes from RRFS and NBM alone and is no higher. I think 0.14 in is about right for this morning; HRRR has under-forecast local bursts before, but even tripling its biggest hour would only just reach the alarm.

Storm totals for the next 72 hours: NBM 0.25 in, ECMWF 0.20, GFS 0.11, RRFS 0.10; the HRRR 15-minute run has 0.40 in from midnight Friday through Saturday night, nearly all of it this morning.

sections.title: Tide and the channel
sections.text:
NOAA's Bay model keeps running about 1.3 to 1.7 ft above the predicted tides. This morning's 7.9 ft high at 8:32 AM runs about 9.5 ft on the model (peaking near 9.6 ft around 9 AM), so the burst falls on a rising, surge-boosted tide that slows the channel's drainage; at these rain rates it should not matter. The 1.2 ft low at 3:15 PM runs about 2.5 ft; the 6.4 ft evening high at 9:15 PM about 8.1 ft. Saturday's 8.4 ft high at 9:06 AM is the highest in the model run at about 9.9 ft. Saturday evening's light rain lines up with the 0.3 ft low at 4:05 PM (about 1.8 ft on the model) and the rising tide toward the 6.6 ft high at 10:19 PM (about 8.1 ft). The model run ends 1 AM Sunday; Sunday's 8.8 ft and Monday's 9.2 ft morning highs are not yet covered.

NWS reissued the Coastal Flood Advisory for Bayshore locations at 3:41 AM, until 11 AM Saturday: up to 1.4 ft of inundation in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways, with up to 1.8 ft of surge. NWS expects to upgrade it to a Coastal Flood Warning on Sunday as the king tides approach.

Channel: upstream of Caltrain the gauge rose from 0.07 ft at 5:13 AM to 0.18 ft at 6:07 AM with the morning showers, far below Flood Monitoring (2.8 ft). At Alameda de las Pulgas it reads 0.27 ft at 7 AM, steady (Flood Monitoring 3.18 ft).

sections.title: Current observations
sections.text: Showers are back on the street. The Caltrain rain gauge has tipped 0.04 in in each of the hours ending 3, 4 and 6 AM, the latest at 6:37 AM: 0.04 in in the last hour, 0.08 in over 3 hours, 0.12 in over 6 hours and 0.24 in over 24 hours. The gauge feed was read at 7:05 AM, so the 7 AM burst the HRRR shows is not in it yet. The channel is low.

sections.title: Uncertainty
sections.text: Low on impact. The models agree that nothing in the next 72 hours comes near the Yellow line; the spread is mostly about whether this morning's showers stay at 0.05 in (RRFS) or reach 0.3 in (HRRR) over a few hours. In cold, unstable air one cell can drop a heavy 15 minutes on one street and miss the next, and NWS keeps a 10% chance of thunderstorms into early afternoon, so a brief downpour near the 8:30 AM high tide is the main wildcard. The missing HRRR hourly data is a gap, but its 15-minute output covers the same hours. Saturday night's rain looks light in every model. Most likely outcome: wet streets and full gutters this morning, then a mostly dry weekend until Saturday evening.

sections.title: What to do
sections.text:
• No need to move cars out of the cul-de-sac.
• Keep an eye on the dashboard until about 10 AM. If the 1-hour burst alarm trips (0.40 in in one hour), move cars and watch the street drain grates.
• Use this afternoon or Monday's dry day to clear leaves from street drain grates and yard drains and check sandbags: Tuesday and Wednesday bring heavier rain with the king tides, and NWS says surge could add to them.
• If water does reach the sidewalk, a timestamped photo at the peak helps tune the dashboard.
• Cold mornings Friday and Saturday. Don't drive or walk through moving water.
